data.text/html:
STUMPY & matrix profiles: find the repeats and the weirdos in any time series

An interactive companion to Sean Law's SciPy 2024 talk "STUMPY: Modern Time Series Analysis with Matrix Profiles".
Someone drops a time series in your lap. Is there any signal, or is it just noise?
Sean's answer in one sentence: compare every subsequence with every other one using plain Pythagoras, keep only the distance to each subsequence's single nearest neighbour, and that one vector — the matrix profile — tells you where behaviour is conserved (low values) and where anomalies hide (high values). Each section below lets you rebuild that idea by hand, in the talk's order.

data.text/markdown:
Colour language (used everywhere below)

■ light blue = the query subsequence you are asking about  ·  ■ dark blue = the subsequence it is compared with / its nearest neighbour  ·  ■ red = distances & discords (anomalies)  ·  ■ orange = motifs (conserved patterns)  ·  ■ grey = the raw series / the excluded "trivial match" zone. Notation from the talk: time series ||(T||) of length ||(n||), window (subsequence length) ||(m||), subsequence ||(T_{i,m} = T[i : i+m]||).

1 · Subsequences and the most boring distance in the world

The talk starts with a tiny series of 13 numbers. Stare at it: do you see a pattern? Probably not yet. Subsequence: just a short section of the full series, ||(T_{i,m} = (t_i, t_{i+1}, \dots, t_{i+m-1})||). Comparing two subsequences: Sean picks the simplest thing he knows, the straight-line (Euclidean) distance. For length 2 it is Pythagoras; for longer windows you just keep adding squared legs: ||[h = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \quad\longrightarrow\quad d(T_{i,m}, T_{j,m}) = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 + \dots}, \qquad a = t_i - t_j,\; b = t_{i+1}-t_{j+1}, \dots||]Identical windows → distance 0; anything else → positive. No magic, no training data, one interpretable parameter ||(m||). Drag the light-blue and dark-blue windows below. The lower panel overlays them; each red dashed leg is one term in the sum.

data.text/markdown:
2 · Brute force: the distance profile

To ask "is this subsequence conserved — does it repeat?", Sean copies the series, pins the light-blue query in place and slides the dark-blue window from the start to the end, writing each Euclidean distance into a vector. That vector is the distance profile of subsequence ||(i||): ||[D_i[j] = d\big(T_{i,m},\, T_{j,m}\big), \qquad j = 0, \dots, n-m.||]It is not an approximation: every comparison is made. Two things to read off it:
  • At ||(j=i||) the distance is 0 — the trivial match (a window matches itself). Neighbouring, overlapping windows are nearly trivial too, so STUMPY ignores an exclusion zone ||(|i-j| \le \lceil m/4 \rceil||) (grey).
  • The smallest value outside that zone is the query's 1-nearest neighbour (dark blue bar).
Pick a query, then press ▶ play and watch the profile being built one slide at a time.

data.text/markdown:
3 · Stack the profiles: distance matrix → matrix profile

Repeat section 2 for every query ||(i||) and stack the profiles: you get the ||((n-m+1)\times(n-m+1)||) distance matrix. Simple, intuitive, exact… and hopeless at scale (see the thermostat calculator below). The 2016 insight (Keogh's lab at UC Riverside & Mueen at UNM): you don't need to keep the matrix. Keep only each row's minimum outside the trivial zone: ||[P[i] = \min_{|j-i| > \lceil m/4\rceil} D_i[j] \qquad\text{(matrix profile)}, \qquad I[i] = \arg\min_j D_i[j] \qquad\text{(matrix profile index)}.||]Still ||(O(n^2)||) time, but only ||(O(n)||) memory — and in STUMPY, with sliding-window tricks, it's fast. Each cell below is one distance; grey = trivial zone; dark-blue outline = the row minimum that survives into ||(P||).

Why nobody computed the full matrix (until now)

Sean's thermostat: one reading every 3 s for 5 years ≈ 52 million points. A naive full distance matrix needs ~||(n^2||) numbers. Play with the inputs; throughput is set so that the defaults reproduce the talk's ≈ 4.4 years, ≈ 11 PB.

Mutual nearest neighbours at the global minimum = the \u003cstrong\u003etop motif\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eFind the tallest bar of \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(P||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e. That window's \u003cem\u003ebest\u003c/em\u003e match is still far away: nothing like it exists elsewhere → a \u003cstrong\u003ediscord\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eIn the calculator, halve the readings per minute: time &amp; matrix memory drop by \u003cstrong\u003e4×\u003c/strong\u003e (quadratic), the profile only by 2× (linear).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
4 · Motifs and discords for free

Amir Mueen & Eamonn Keogh's claim (quoted in the talk): "given a matrix profile, most time series data mining problems are trivial to solve in a few lines of code." The two most important ones:
  • Motif (conserved behaviour) = the global minimum of ||(P||). Its index ||(I||) points at the matching window.
  • Discord (potential anomaly) = the global maximum of ||(P||): the window whose best match is still bad.
Below is a 1,000-point series, the kind that "lands in your lap". A pattern was hidden in it twice, plus one glitch. Predict first: where does a repeated pattern start? Lock your guess, then STUMPY reveals the answer.
T_demo: n = 1000 points (seeded, generated in-notebook).

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eShrink \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(m||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e to 8–12: the motif shrinks to a fragment of the pattern, and the glitch dominates more.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eGrow \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(m||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e to 100+: the windows now contain the pattern \u003cem\u003eplus\u003c/em\u003e random noise, so the motif's \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(P||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e value rises — the match gets blurrier.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNotice the nearest neighbour can be in the \u003cstrong\u003epast or the future\u003c/strong\u003e — \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(I||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e points both ways.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · The asterisk: z-normalisation

From the Q&A: the matrix profile definition had a small asterisk — z-normalised. Before measuring, STUMPY rescales each window: ||[\hat T_{i,m} = \frac{T_{i,m} - \mu_i}{\sigma_i} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad d_z(i,j) = \sqrt{2m\,(1-\rho_{ij})},||]where ||(\rho_{ij}||) is the Pearson correlation of the two windows. So the distance cares about shape, not level or amplitude — no detrending or differencing needed. It's on by default; stumpy.stump(T, m, normalize=False) turns it off. Below, the pattern from the query window (light blue, i = 80) reappears later 3× taller on a rising trend. Which mode finds it?

<marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eFlip the switch off. Raw Euclidean distance picks a nearby flat stretch at a similar \u003cem\u003elevel\u003c/em\u003e instead of the true copy.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eCompare the last two numbers: with z-normalisation, \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(d = \\sqrt{2m(1-\\rho)}||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e exactly. Raw mode breaks that identity.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eWhen is raw better? When \u003cem\u003eamplitude itself\u003c/em\u003e matters (e.g. a temperature exceeding 40 °C is the event). Because STUMPY is fast, Sean's advice is: try both.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Which window size ||(m||)? The pan matrix profile

The most common question to the researchers: how do I choose ||(m||)? Because computing a profile is cheap, compute it for many ||(m||), divide each by its maximum possible z-normalised distance ||(2\sqrt m||) so they're comparable, and stack them: the pan matrix profile. Paint every value below a threshold black. Dark "triangles" mark where conserved behaviour lives and over which range of window lengths.

data.text/markdown:
7 · Sandbox: draw your own time series

Paint a series with the mouse (click-drag across the canvas), or start from a preset. On release, STUMPY computes the matrix profile and marks the top motif pair (orange) and the top discord (red). Your job: fool it, or make it find what you meant.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eChallenges\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePure noise\u003c/strong\u003e: the motif/discord ratio collapses toward ~1–2 — the matrix profile is telling you \u003cem\u003e\"no conserved behaviour here\"\u003c/em\u003e (Sean's first question!).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSine + glitch\u003c/strong\u003e: the discord lands on the spike at i = 110. Now paint a \u003cem\u003esecond\u003c/em\u003e identical spike elsewhere — the discord moves, because a repeated anomaly is no longer anomalous.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTwo hidden bumps\u003c/strong\u003e: set \u003cmarimo-tex class=\"arithmatex\"\u003e||(m||)\u003c/marimo-tex\u003e to the bump width (~30) and check the motif pair lands at 30 ↔ 140. Then draw a third bump \u003cem\u003eupside-down\u003c/em\u003e: z-normalisation can't call that a match.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

Beyond this notebook (all in STUMPY): AB-joins between two series, streaming updates (stumpy.stumpi), fast pattern matching (stumpy.match), top-k nearest neighbours (k=), approximate profiles (scrump), and multi-dimensional motifs (mstump). Sean's call to action: put those three lines into your exploratory data analysis before you reach for a model.
